metadata.title: The Mechanics of Conformity: Structural Similarities Between Distributed Social Enforcement and Authoritarian Control
metadata.description:
This paper examines whether centralized state authoritarianism and distributed social enforcement in democratic societies — commonly termed "cancel culture" — produce structurally comparable conformity pressures despite relying on different institutional mechanisms. Centralized authoritarian regimes rely on formal state coercion, legal monopolies, and physical sanctions; contemporary democratic societies instead experience reputational and administrative pressure operating through networked digital platforms and institutional risk management.

The paper draws on faculty-targeting and self-censorship survey data from FIRE, AAUP/AAC&U/NORC, and Knight Foundation–Ipsos; state-legislation data from PEN America; academic survey research by Norris (2023) and Heterodox Academy (2024); and the authors' own original analysis of two primary microdata sources — General Social Survey political-tolerance data (1977–2024) and V-Dem's Academic Freedom Index (1900–2025) — processed directly from public-use files rather than cited secondhand. From this evidence, the paper proposes a ten-stage descriptive model of how moralized boundary-framing, institutional risk-aversion, and preference falsification can combine to chill speech. It also considers — without asserting as empirically proven — how these dynamics could in principle be exploited by organized actors for administrative capture, and reviews evidence indicating this pattern is not confined to one part of the political spectrum, nor uniform across institutional or national contexts. The paper concludes with proposed institutional safeguards, flagged as untested proposals rather than validated interventions.

Notes

This consolidated draft has gone through five revision passes. The original two recovered fragments were merged, missing prose restored, and empirical figures corrected against primary sources (RC1). Later passes integrated PEN America state-legislation data and a Knight Foundation–Ipsos probability-sample survey, and distinguished direct state action from distributed social enforcement within the paper's own analytic framework (RC2). The most recent passes added original analysis of primary microdata supplied by the author — General Social Survey political-tolerance data, 1977–2024 (RC3–RC4), and V-Dem's Academic Freedom Index, 1900–2025 (RC5) — both parsed, validated, and analyzed directly from public-use files rather than taken from a secondary summary. Added empirical claims are cited; retained conceptual passages without added citations reflect the original framework rather than independently verified findings.

Method

Conceptual and theoretical synthesis, supported by (a) secondary empirical sources including FIRE faculty-targeting and self-censorship data, AAUP/AAC&U/NORC academic-freedom survey data, PEN America state-legislation tracking, Knight Foundation–Ipsos survey data, and research by Norris (2023), Heterodox Academy (2024), Chong/Citrin/Levy (2022), and Mutz (2023); and (b) original quantitative analysis of two primary microdata sources processed directly from their public-use files: General Social Survey political-tolerance microdata (1977–2024, 24 survey years, weighted) and V-Dem Academic Freedom Index microdata (1900–2025). The ten-stage conformity model is descriptive, not a directly tested causal chain; the two original microdata analyses carry methodological notes on data processing and validation and are clearly distinguished in-text from cited secondary statistics.
keywords: cancel culture; distributed social enforcement; authoritarianism; conformity; academic freedom; self-censorship; DEI; institutional risk-aversion; preference falsification; spiral of silence; administrative capture

metadata.title: African Literature in the Digital Age: Social Media, Identity and Literary Expression in Francophone Africa
metadata.description:
This paper examines how social media and digital technologies are transforming literary production, circulation, identity construction, and linguistic expression in contemporary Francophone Africa. It argues that the digital turn has created a hybrid literary ecology in which print culture, oral performance, African languages, French, audiovisual media, and networked communication interact. Drawing on postcolonial theory, cultural identity studies, and digital literary scholarship, the study investigates the changing relationship between writers and readers, the construction of transnational identities, linguistic hybridity, digital literary forms, feminist agency, political expression, and the coloniality of data. The paper contends that social media can reduce dependence on conventional publishing gatekeepers and expand access to literary publics, while simultaneously producing new forms of algorithmic, commercial, and technological gatekeeping. In Francophone Africa, digital writing therefore represents neither an unqualified liberation nor a simple continuation of colonial domination. Rather, it constitutes a contested cultural space in which writer’s appropriate digital technologies to negotiate language, identity, memory, belonging, and power. The study concludes that the future of Francophone African literature will be increasingly multimodal and transnational, requiring literary scholarship to address both the creative possibilities and structural inequalities of digital culture.

Keywords: Francophone Africa; African literature; social media; digital humanities; identity; literary expression; linguistic hybridity.

metadata.title: THE IMPACT OF EARLY DIAGNOSIS ON CLINICAL OUTCOMES IN PEDIATRIC DILATED CARDIOMYOPATHY
metadata.description: Dilated cardiomyopathy is a severe, life-threatening myocardial disease in the pediatric population, frequently characterized by a delayed clinical presentation that severely limits therapeutic efficacy. This extensive observational research investigates the critical impact of early versus late diagnosis on the long-term clinical outcomes, myocardial reverse remodeling, and overall survival rates in a cohort of forty-eight pediatric patients. The clinical investigation was conducted at the Andijan Regional Children's Multidisciplinary Medical Center. The patient cohort was stratified into an early diagnosis group and a late diagnosis group based on the duration of symptoms prior to specialized cardiological intervention and the baseline severity of heart failure. The comprehensive analysis demonstrates that early echocardiographic detection and the subsequent immediate initiation of neurohormonal blockade significantly correlate with higher rates of complete left ventricular functional recovery, dramatically reduced incidences of life-threatening arrhythmias, and superior long-term survival. The findings unequivocally underscore the necessity of implementing rigorous, early echocardiographic screening protocols in primary pediatric care to identify subclinical myocardial dysfunction, thereby shifting the treatment paradigm from palliative heart failure management to active disease modification and structural preservation.

metadata.title: Parameter Sensitivity Algebra (ASP) within the Preference Propagation Framework (PPF)
metadata.description:
This record presents a proposed formulation of Parameter Sensitivity Algebra (ASP) for extracting criterion-specific parameter elasticities from representative equations. For an additive positive model, parameter elasticity is decomposed into structural sensitivity and a context-dependent term-participation factor. The resulting elasticity matrix may subsequently be used by the Preference Propagation Framework (PPF) to propagate declared criterion orientations and weights toward a Unified Preference Representation (UPR).

The formulation is presented as a theoretical and computational proposal. Exact differential identities are distinguished from local monomial representations and from empirical validation. Independent mathematical review, computational benchmarking, and domain-expert validation remain necessary.

AI systems were used as analytical assistants for equation checking, counterexample exploration, terminology refinement, and documentation. Their outputs do not constitute independent scientific validation or institutional endorsement.

metadata.title: Open Logic Project — Türkçe Tam Sürüm / Complete Turkish Edition (OLP-0722, 722/722)
metadata.description:
Complete Turkish edition: all 722/722 frozen Open Logic Project content modules are translated. The 1,037-page linked reader covers the 642 canonical-reader-reachable modules; 80 retained non-reader modules remain in the editable corpus and are explicitly outside build/render applicability. Frozen authority: commit 9620cc73f9c8e0ad003c514a5d3748f29611c4c0, tree f67757bb9305b173634082ab4cefd5601a707a34, under CC BY 4.0.

All 722 targets passed aggregate exact-source, structural, and model-review admission. The 642 reader-reachable targets additionally passed a deterministic build with exit code 0 and zero missing-character or unresolved-reference/citation diagnostics, complete text-layer residue scans, and all-page visual inspection; build/render are not applicable to the 80 retained non-reader targets. metadata.description: This dataset contains supplementary data and analysis files supporting the manuscript “Ecological sorting of ancient RuBisCO lineages structures Earth’s microbial carbon-fixation potential.” The files include curated genome metadata, habitat annotations, functional profiles, RbcL sequences and alignments, phylogenetic trees, residue-level metrics, predicted RbcL structural models, COM-derived structural descriptors, ancestral-state reconstruction analyses of RbcL-associated metabolic traits, phylogenetic signal analyses, PGLS model outputs, and bacterial–eukaryotic Form I reference analyses. The updated version additionally includes Datasets S7, containing the trait matrix, rooted RbcL tree, ancestral-state likelihood estimates, key-node summaries, and sensitivity analyses underlying the ancestral-state reconstructions.

metadata.title: Dynamic Response Suppression in Metamaterials: Structural Design, Mechanisms, and Transmissibility
metadata.description:
This dataset provides the primary supporting data for our latest review paper, "Dynamic Response Suppression in Metamaterials: Structural Design, Mechanisms, and Transmissibility".

The literature-derived data are compiled in ZenodoDataset_Updated.xlsx, which includes detailed informantion extracted from the reviewed studies, such as bandgap data from Bloch-based dispersion analyses, transmissibility-based bandgaps, experimental validation details, and material specifications. 

The file Sec3_Plots.py serves as the script to generate Figure 10 to 12 in our paper. All corresponding data points have been listed directly in the script, allowing readers to reproduce the unprocessed Ashby plots by running the code in a Python environment.
